studyTasks: Read the notes for {topic} and highlight definitions, examples, and teacher-emphasized details.
Build a one-page study sheet for {topic} with key terms, steps, and one worked example.
Explain {topic} in your own words, then compare your explanation to your notes.
stepTasks: List what you know, fill gaps from notes, then write a clean explanation without looking.
Choose two class examples, label each step, then make one similar example of your own.
Create a mini concept map connecting {topic} to at least two other test topics.
practiceTasks: Complete {practiceCount} focused questions about {topic}; include at least two that feel challenging.
Make {practiceCount} self-test questions about {topic}, answer them, then check with your notes.
Do a mixed set that includes {topic} plus one older topic so you practice switching skills.
mistakeChecks: Write every mistake in a mistake log with the correct answer and the reason it is correct.
Redo missed questions from memory after checking the answer.
Circle the exact step or idea that caused confusion and write a fix-it note.
miniReviews: Close your notes and write five facts, steps, or examples you remember about {topic}.
Make three quick flashcards for the hardest ideas from {topic}.
End with a two-minute spoken explanation of {topic}.

studyTasks: Read notes for {topic} and build a formula, vocabulary, and example sheet.
Copy one correct worked example for {topic}, then annotate why each step happens.
Sort {topic} problems by type so you know which method to choose.
stepTasks: Write the rule or formula, solve one guided example, then solve one without looking.
Make a decision guide for choosing the right method on {topic} questions.
Compare two problem types and write the first step for each.
practiceTasks: Solve {practiceCount} problems on {topic}; show each step and check your answer.
Complete {practiceCount} questions with at least two word problems or graph-based questions.
Do a timed set of {practiceCount} mixed questions, then mark slow or uncertain steps.
mistakeChecks: Redo every missed problem and write the correct first step beside it.
Label mistakes as formula, sign, setup, graph, or arithmetic errors.
Choose the two hardest misses and solve them again without notes.
miniReviews: Make five flashcards for formulas, vocabulary, or common first steps.
Write a final rule sheet for {topic} from memory, then fill in missing pieces.
Explain one solved example out loud as if teaching it.

studyTasks: Review notes for {topic}, then draw or label the most important diagram or process.
Create a cause/effect chain for {topic} using arrows and short explanations.
Build a vocabulary list for {topic} with examples, not just definitions.
stepTasks: Define key terms, sketch the process, then explain what changes at each stage.
Connect {topic} to one lab, demonstration, or real-world application.
Write three cause/effect statements and one exception or special case.
practiceTasks: Answer {practiceCount} concept, process, and application questions about {topic}.
Label or redraw the main diagram, then answer {practiceCount} questions about it.
Complete a short lab/application question set and explain evidence for each answer.
mistakeChecks: Mark confused vocabulary and rewrite definitions with an example.
Redraw any missed diagram or process without looking.
Explain why each wrong answer is wrong, especially for cause/effect questions.
miniReviews: Quiz yourself on key terms, then explain the process in order.
Make a quick diagram from memory and check missing labels.
Write three sentences connecting {topic} to another science idea.

studyTasks: Review notes for {topic} and build a thesis, quote, and evidence bank.
Identify the strongest themes or arguments for {topic} and match each with evidence.
Study paragraph structure for {topic}: topic sentence, evidence, explanation, closing link.
stepTasks: Write one thesis, choose two quotes, then explain how each quote proves the point.
Create a paragraph outline before writing any full sentences.
Revise one weak explanation so it connects evidence back to the thesis.
practiceTasks: Draft {practiceCount} paragraph outlines or short responses using evidence.
Write one complete paragraph about {topic} and highlight claim, evidence, and analysis.
Practice integrating {practiceCount} quotes smoothly with context and explanation.
mistakeChecks: Check for summary-only writing and add analysis where needed.
Underline unclear thesis wording and rewrite it more directly.
Make sure every quote has an explanation, not just placement.
miniReviews: Recite your thesis and two pieces of evidence without looking.
Make a mini outline for a possible test prompt.
Review transition words and sentence starters for analysis.

studyTasks: Review notes for {topic} and create a timeline, map, or cause/effect chart.
Build a key term list for {topic} with people, places, dates, and consequences.
Compare two events, regions, or viewpoints connected to {topic}.
stepTasks: Put events in order, label causes and effects, then write a short significance statement.
Read one source or map, identify the main message, and connect it to your notes.
Make a compare/contrast chart with at least three similarities or differences.
practiceTasks: Answer {practiceCount} key term, source, map, or compare/contrast questions.
Write one short response explaining causes, effects, and evidence for {topic}.
Practice reading a map, chart, or source and write what it proves.
mistakeChecks: Fix mixed-up dates, places, or terms by adding them to a timeline.
Rewrite vague cause/effect answers with specific evidence.
Review any source question you missed and identify the clue you overlooked.
miniReviews: Recall the timeline or map from memory, then check gaps.
Make five flashcards for key terms, people, places, or causes.
Write a three-sentence summary of why {topic} matters.

studyTasks: Review notes for {topic} and pair each concept with a real or class example.
Build a vocabulary sheet for {topic} with definitions and business examples.
Study how {topic} affects decisions, costs, customers, or strategy.
stepTasks: Define the concept, give an example, then explain the business decision it supports.
Read a short case or scenario and identify the problem, option, and best action.
Make a chart connecting vocabulary to examples and possible test questions.
practiceTasks: Complete {practiceCount} application or case-study questions about {topic}.
Answer scenario questions where you must choose and justify a business decision.
Practice vocabulary by writing examples and non-examples for each term.
mistakeChecks: Rewrite vague answers with a specific concept, example, and result.
Check whether each answer applies the term instead of only defining it.
Redo one case question and justify the decision with evidence.
miniReviews: Explain {topic} using a real business example.
Make flashcards for terms and one-line applications.
Write one possible test question and a model answer.

studyTasks: Review vocabulary and grammar notes for {topic}, then make example sentences.
Group vocabulary for {topic} by theme and add one useful phrase for each group.
Study the grammar pattern for {topic} and write the rule in your own words.
stepTasks: Read the rule, copy two correct examples, then write three original sentences.
Practice saying key phrases aloud, then write them without looking.
Translate short sentences both ways and mark grammar changes.
practiceTasks: Complete {practiceCount} speaking, writing, grammar, or reading tasks for {topic}.
Write {practiceCount} original sentences using vocabulary and grammar from {topic}.
Read a short passage or prompt and answer questions using full sentences.
mistakeChecks: Correct spelling, accents, agreement, and word order mistakes.
Rewrite incorrect sentences and underline the changed grammar.
Say the corrected sentence aloud three times.
miniReviews: Quiz yourself on vocabulary, then write five sentences from memory.
Record or say a short response using {topic}.
Make a tiny grammar card with the rule and one example.
